clue.text: Goddess at one time packing case in America

indicators.note: Packing something means carrying it around inside your luggage, so one word travels within another.
A case is the shell a thing sits in, so what is kept is the shell of the word — the letter at each end.

parts.note: the country begins and ends with the same letter, which makes a tidy shell
'at one time' = then, back in the day

explanation.surface: A goddess who once travelled across America with her case packed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' is the suitcase the surface is packing and a word's outer shell in the wordplay — packaging words are how setters ask for first-and-last letters, and America is a generous one.
explanation.definitionFit: ATHENA is the Greek goddess of wisdom and war, so 'Goddess' is the category she belongs to rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Bottle consumed by familiar artist

indicators.note: To be consumed is to be swallowed whole, so the shorter word disappears inside the longer one.

parts.note: a familiar is a friend, and a mate is what you call one
in British slang bottle is nerve, and so is grit

explanation.surface: A painter's bottle being drunk by an old friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' is British slang for nerve, with no drink in it, and 'familiar' is a noun here — the mate the surface is sitting with.
explanation.definitionFit: MAGRITTE painted the bowler hats and the pipe labelled 'this is not a pipe', so 'artist' is the class he is being placed in.

clue.text: Artist, artist after split

indicators.note: 'After' means later in the line, so the piece it introduces is written second, behind what is already down.

parts.note: to rive is to split or tear apart
RA = Royal Academician, the crossword's stock painter

explanation.surface: One painter trailing another after a break-up.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'artist' appears twice and means something different each time: the first is what you are hunting for, the second is the Royal Academician setters use for any painter at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Diego RIVERA covered Mexico's public buildings in murals, so 'Artist' names the category he sits in.

clue.text: Bacon paintings hard for artist

parts.note: bacon comes off a hog
paintings are art
H is the grade stamped on a hard pencil

explanation.surface: Francis Bacon's canvases proving hard going for a fellow painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Capitalised, Bacon is Francis Bacon the painter on the surface and a pig underneath — the sort of proper-noun disguise this grid uses again and again.
explanation.definitionFit: William HOGARTH engraved A Rake's Progress and Gin Lane, so the definition places him in the general class of artists.

clue.text: Wife and artist keeping pea, essentially, in pod

definitions.note: 'Pod' is singular and names a group, while the answer is plural: the setter is defining the animals by the collective noun for a school of them.

indicators.note: To keep something is to hold on to it, so the small piece stays held inside the word that keeps it.

parts.note: W = wife, a standard abbreviation

indicators.note: The essence of a word is what sits at its heart, so this takes the middle letter and nothing else.

parts.note: Frans Hals, the Dutch portraitist who painted the Laughing Cavalier
the middle letter of pEa

explanation.surface: A wife and a painter minding one pea in its pod.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a collective noun rather than a synonym — the group standing in for the creatures that make it up — which is why 'in pod' reads as part of the vegetable picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A pod is the collective noun for WHALES travelling together, so they are defined by the group they swim in.

clue.text: Artist in clover, one senses

indicators.note: 'In' is being literal: the letters are sitting inside the words that follow, already in the right order.

parts.note: eight letters in a row, starting four letters into the first word, crossing a comma and two gaps

explanation.surface: A painter living in luxury, or so somebody suspects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In clover' is an idiom for living comfortably, which is exactly why it never reads as an instruction, and 'one senses' rounds off the picture instead of hinting at concealment.
explanation.definitionFit: Paolo VERONESE filled Venetian walls with enormous banquet scenes, so 'Artist' is the category the clue drops him into.

clue.text: Smoother artist after ammo initially loading type of gun

indicators.note: 'After' fixes the order: what follows the word goes behind the piece already named.

parts.note: the Sten was the British army's cheap wartime submachine gun

indicators.note: 'Initially' means at the very start, so only the opening letter of the word beside it is taken.
A gun is loaded by pushing something down inside it, which is where these letters end up.

parts.note: the first letter of Ammo
Joan Miró, the Catalan painter of floating shapes

explanation.surface: An artist packing ammunition into a gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoother' is a noun — the thing that does the smoothing — rather than the comparative adjective it looks like, and the Sten is standard crossword hardware.
explanation.definitionFit: A STEAM IRON is a smoother in the plainest sense: you push it over cloth to take the creases out.

clue.text: Turner on The Hay Wain?

parts.note: the surface offers J.M.W. Turner, one more painter in a grid stuffed with them
Constable's painting shows a farm wagon standing in a ford — look at what it rolls along on

explanation.surface: One famous English painter apparently turning up in another's masterpiece.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here separates into wordplay: the capital T sells you a painter's name where the clue means a thing that goes round, and a hay wain rides on four of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A WHEEL is a turner in the literal sense — an object whose whole purpose is to rotate — with no metaphor involved.

clue.text: Rescuing relative at sea, Romeo saved

indicators.note: Anything at sea is adrift with nothing holding its position, which is what happens to these letters.
'Saved' here means kept rather than pulled from the water, so the extra letter is retained in the mix.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
R = Romeo in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A family member adrift in the water and a man called Romeo brought safely home.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo is the NATO alphabet's R, not the lover, and 'at sea' works both ways at once — the shipwreck in the picture, and the instruction that the letters have come loose.
explanation.definitionFit: RETRIEVAL is the act of getting something back, which is what rescuing amounts to when the thing recovered is a person.

clue.text: Sailing boat in lottery capsized

indicators.note: A capsized boat has gone right over, so the letters are read from the far end back.

parts.note: the pools are Britain's weekly bet on football results, a lottery in all but name; 'capsized' turns the word round

explanation.surface: A boat going over while the week's lottery is drawn.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'lottery' as the national draw with the numbered balls; the pools came first, and it is that older word the clue turns over.
explanation.definitionFit: A SLOOP is a single-masted sailing boat, so the definition names it by its category rather than any special feature.

clue.text: Sport in which artist has lost tie

indicators.note: What is lost is gone from what remains, so those three letters are simply missing from the name.

parts.note: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, the Venetian who frescoed ceilings across eighteenth-century Europe
the three letters T, I and E are what goes, and they happen to sit at the very front

explanation.surface: A painter knocked out of a cup tie in some sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sport in which' looks like the start of a container — something tucked inside the game — and it is only joinery holding the sentence up. 'Tie' is a cup match on the surface and three letters underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: POLO is the stick-and-ball game played on horseback, so 'Sport' is the category name standing in for it.

clue.text: Artist not entirely impressed by intro of traditional chant that's sacred

indicators.note: 'Not entirely' stops you short of the finish, so the name arrives one letter shy of complete.
An intro is the opening, so nothing but the first letter of the word after it is used.

parts.note: Man Ray, the American surrealist, docked of his last letter

indicators.note: To be impressed by something is to have it stamped into you, which is how the single letter gets inside.

parts.note: the first letter of Traditional

explanation.surface: A painter half-persuaded by the opening of an old sacred chant.
explanation.walkthrough: The last two letters look like the Royal Academician this grid leans on again and again; they are the tail of a photographer's surname instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A MANTRA is a sacred formula chanted in Hindu and Buddhist practice, so the definition reads straight with nothing bent.

clue.text: Told hoes (or hose), or those old screws — here?

definitions.note: 'Here' is an adverb pointing at a place while the answer names one, and the question mark carries the setter's gesture at where all this clutter is kept.

indicators.note: To screw something up is to twist it out of shape, and twisted letters no longer sit in the order they were handed to you.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
swap the last two letters and the same eight are offered a second time
a third arrangement of the identical eight letters, with the setter enjoying himself

explanation.surface: Somebody reeling off a list of old garden gear and rusty fixings.
explanation.walkthrough: The same eight letters are handed over three times in one sentence, and 'screws' finishes the shopping list while quietly issuing the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoes, hose and old screws are exactly what a TOOL SHED holds, so 'here' points at the building they are all kept in.

clue.text: Tissue cut then by artist

indicators.note: Something cut is shortened, so the word arrives with its final letter trimmed off.

parts.note: Paul Klee, the Swiss-German painter of the Twittering Machine
'then' in the sense of next, with the last letter taken off

explanation.surface: A tissue snipped up beside a working painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks as though it belongs to the tissue and belongs to 'then' instead, which is standing in for the word NEXT. The definition works because a brand name has become the everyday noun.
explanation.definitionFit: KLEENEX is a trademark that turned into the ordinary word for a paper tissue, so the definition names the thing by its best-known brand.

clue.text: Artist excited ship's lookout?

parts.note: after weeks at sea the one sight that gets a crew shouting is the shore
a seer is one who sees, which is the whole of a lookout's job

explanation.surface: A man at the masthead yelling about what he can see.
explanation.walkthrough: A lookout who has just sighted the coast is a land-seer, and that is the whole of the wordplay — no letters move. Edwin Landseer painted the Victorians' stags and modelled the Trafalgar Square lions.
explanation.definitionFit: Edwin LANDSEER was the Victorians' favourite animal painter, so 'Artist' names the class he belongs to.

clue.text: Artist, sign unframed?

indicators.note: A picture out of its frame has lost the border round the edge, so the first and last letters go.

parts.note: the zodiac sign of the twins

explanation.surface: An artist's signature hung on the wall without a frame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign' is the zodiac rather than a signature, and 'unframed' is a picture-gallery word doing a letter's job. Tracey Emin's unmade bed and neon texts are the work behind the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Tracey EMIN is one of the Young British Artists, so 'Artist' is the category rather than any description of what she makes.

clue.text: Wood nailed back by bloody artist

indicators.note: Nailing a plank drives it into whatever it is fixed to, so those letters end up buried inside the other word.

parts.note: bloody = gory

indicators.note: In an across entry, back is right to left, so the timber's letters are read the other way.

parts.note: the elm is a timber tree; 'back' turns its three letters round

explanation.surface: A short-tempered painter hammering a plank back into place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' is the swearword in the surface and plain gore in the wordplay. Antony Gormley made the Angel of the North, the giant steel figure beside the road at Gateshead.
explanation.definitionFit: GORMLEY is a sculptor, and 'artist' covers sculptors as readily as painters — a category name for a maker of art of any kind.

clue.text: Manet or Hockney originally turned over

indicators.note: Something turned has been spun into a new arrangement, so the letters do not stay as they were given.
'Originally' means at the outset, so only the opening letter of the name beside it is taken.

parts.note: anagram fodder — the painter's name plus the little word joining him to the next
the first letter of Hockney

explanation.surface: Two painters' names being flipped over on a gallery label.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like a choice between two painters and supplies two of the eight letters, and the definition is the single last word, which reads as half of 'turned over'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Over' in the counting sense — over fifty, over budget — is exactly MORE THAN, and the two swap in freely.

clue.text: Questionable claims come up briefly for artist

indicators.note: 'Briefly' means cut short, so the word gives up its final letter before it goes anywhere.
To claim something is to take it in as your own, so the shorter piece is held inside the longer word.

parts.note: a moot point is a questionable one, still open to argument
to come up is to rise, and the E drops off the end

explanation.surface: Dubious allegations surfacing briefly about a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come up' is not a reversal instruction, even in a down clue — it is the word RISE, trimmed. Berthe Morisot was the leading woman among the Impressionists.
explanation.definitionFit: Berthe MORISOT showed at nearly every Impressionist exhibition, so 'artist' is the category the clue puts her in.

clue.text: Artist in cage with lion torn to pieces

indicators.note: Something torn to pieces is in bits, and bits can be put back together in any order at all.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A painter shut in a cage with a lion and torn apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In cage' reads as an insertion — someone tucked inside — when the cage is supplying letters rather than holding any. Fra Angelico was a Dominican friar as well as a painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Fra ANGELICO painted altarpieces and frescoes in fifteenth-century Florence, so 'Artist' is the class he is named by.

clue.text: Brow wiped of female, say, stealing a charm

indicators.note: The brow is the top of a face, and the top of a down entry is its first letter, so wiping it takes the head off the word.
To steal something is to take it in and keep it, so the single letter is tucked away inside.

parts.note: female is one example of a gender, and 'say' turns the example into the category; then the leading G is wiped away
used literally

explanation.surface: A woman's forehead being mopped dry while a lucky charm goes missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Female, say' works upwards from an example to the class it belongs to, which is the reverse of the usual definition-by-example. 'Brow' is positional, and a down clue's brow is where it starts.
explanation.definitionFit: To ENDEAR someone is to make them liked, which is 'charm' as a verb — the winning-over sense, not the amulet the surface dangles.

clue.text: Whistler recalled mother having little time for theorist

indicators.note: To recall is to call back, and in an across entry back means the letters run right to left.

parts.note: the official who blows the whistle at a match; 'recalled' turns the three letters round
ma is the familiar word for mother
t is the short form of time, as on a stopwatch

explanation.surface: Whistler thinking back to his mother, who had no patience with some theorist.
explanation.walkthrough: Whistler's Mother is the painting the surface is trading on, while the whistler in the wordplay blows for offside. Pierre de Fermat did his number theory as a spare-time lawyer.
explanation.definitionFit: FERMAT proved and conjectured his way through number theory, so 'theorist' names him by the work rather than by any title he held.

clue.text: Foxtrot is the dancing obsession

parts.note: F is Foxtrot in the NATO alphabet

indicators.note: Letters that are dancing are moving about the floor and will not be standing where they started.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: The foxtrot being the one dance everybody is mad about.
explanation.walkthrough: Foxtrot is the NATO alphabet's F, so the dance hands over a single letter, and the two words a solver would skip straight past are the ones on the move.
explanation.definitionFit: A FETISH is a fixation somebody cannot leave alone, which is 'obsession' in its everyday sense.

clue.text: In a particular way, what a lone ranger might need?

parts.note: he is one man riding by himself, and the article for one is spelt this way in front of a vowel
what somebody out on their own is short of is a friend on their side

explanation.surface: A ranger riding alone who could do with some company.
explanation.walkthrough: Answer the question aloud and the two words run together into a single adverb: AN + ALLY. 'Particular' is the fussy, detail-obsessed sense, not 'specific'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ANAL is obsessively particular about detail, so doing a thing ANALLY is doing it in exactly that fussy manner.

clue.text: Whisper first song on record?

parts.note: the first of anything is its A — the A-list, the A-team, the A-road
a record has two of these and the songs sit on them

explanation.surface: The opening track on somebody's record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whisper' is a noun here — the remark, not the act of murmuring — and the lead track of a single goes on the A-side.
explanation.definitionFit: An ASIDE is a remark dropped quietly so that only some hear it, which is a whisper in the theatrical sense.

clue.text: Artist, it's time to check out food expert!

parts.note: to check out is to leave for good
Titian, the Venetian master whose name is also a shade of red hair

explanation.surface: A painter being told to go and take a look at some food expert.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is an order shouted at a painter, which is why the pieces arrive in the clue back to front. 'Check out' means take a look on the surface and something far more final underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A DIETITIAN is trained to advise on what people should eat, so 'food expert' describes the profession rather than naming it.

clue.text: Artist burst bubble, in a manner of speaking?

indicators.note: The phrase owns up to the looseness: the name is being read as an invented verb rather than used strictly.

parts.note: DE- is the prefix that undoes a thing, as in defrost or derail
a bubble is a pocket of it, and bursting lets that out

explanation.surface: A painter poking at a bubble until it pops.
explanation.walkthrough: To de-gas something is to take the gas out of it, which is what popping a bubble does. The painter's name is said nothing like the verb hiding inside it — day-GAH, not the two flat syllables.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgar DEGAS painted the ballet dancers and racecourses of Paris, so 'Artist' is the category rather than a description.

clue.text: Artifice still for artist

parts.note: a con is a trick — artifice in its dishonest sense
something stable does not move, which is what still means here

explanation.surface: Trickery still going on in the art world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' is the adjective meaning motionless, not the adverb meaning yet, and that swap hides six of the nine letters. John Constable painted The Hay Wain, which 8 across is standing on.
explanation.definitionFit: John CONSTABLE painted the Suffolk countryside he grew up in, so 'artist' is the general class he is named by.
